# Deep coal mining (drainage, ventilation, safety lamp) (`coal_mining`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/energy.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Energy & engines (`energy`)
- Deps: helped by piston_pump, atmospheric_engine, animal_power_gin, railway
- Core idea: Coal lies in seams; below the outcrop it is reached by shafts and worked by leaving pillars of coal to hold the roof (pillar and stall) or by taking it all along a face and letting the roof settle behind (longwall), with timber props. Three things limit depth. Water: drained by an adit to a valley, else pumped. Air: sink two shafts and keep a fire at the foot of one, so its hot air rises and pulls fresh air down the other, and steer that current past every working place with doors and partitions. Gas: firedamp (methane) is lighter than air, gathers under the roof and explodes when it makes up 5 to 15 % of the air; chokedamp (carbon dioxide and nitrogen) is heavy, lies on the floor and puts out a candle and a man; after an explosion carbon monoxide kills the survivors. A safety lamp encloses the flame in fine wire gauze (about 28 wires to the inch), which cools the flame so that it cannot pass outward.
- Pitfalls:
  - A single shaft: no air circuit and no second way out
  - Believing the Davy lamp made mines safe; it let owners work gassier seams, and its gauze passes flame in a fast draught or when red hot
  - Thinning or removing pillars to get more coal
  - Rushing in after an explosion; afterdamp (carbon monoxide) kills rescuers. A caged bird gives warning
  - Ignoring coal dust, which explodes on its own once stirred up
- History: china: coal burnt from Han times (2nd c. BC or earlier); main fuel of the Northern Song iron industry in the 11th c.; described to Europe by Marco Polo c. 1298; rome: 2nd–4th c. AD – outcrop coal used in Roman Britain for forges and heating; europe: c. 1195 – coal dug at Liège; 13th c. sea coal shipped from Newcastle to London; 1712 Newcomen engine drains pits; 1760s Spedding at Whitehaven courses the air; 1815 safety lamps of Davy, George Stephenson and Clanny; 1906 Courrières disaster shows the danger of coal dust; americas: pre-Columbian – Hopi dig coal for pottery firing in Arizona (c. 13th c.); commercial mining in Virginia from the 1740s
- Read:
  - Georgius Agricola, De re metallica (1556; tr. H. C. Hoover & L. H. Hoover, 1912)
  - Humphry Davy, On the Fire-Damp of Coal Mines, and on Methods of Lighting the Mines So as to Prevent Its Explosion, Phil. Trans. 106 (1816)
  - Michael W. Flinn, The History of the British Coal Industry, Vol. 2: 1700–1830, The Industrial Revolution (1984)
